RAG evaluation: How would you separate a: Evaluate the stages independently so a good final answer does not hide weak retrieval. For retrieval, measure metrics such as recall@k, precision@k, MRR, and nDCG against queries with known relevant chunks. For generation, measure faithfulness to retrieved context, citation correctness, completeness, and refusal behavior when context is insufficient. For end-to-end quality, use a representative golden dataset, task-specific correctness rubrics, human review, and production feedback. Slice results by query type, tenant, language, and document source, and retain the retrieved chunks, prompt version, and model version for every failed case.
RAG ingestion: How would you update a la: Treat the embedding model and chunking configuration as versioned index dependencies. Build the new index or collection in parallel, process inserts, updates, and tombstones idempotently, and validate freshness plus retrieval quality against a golden set. Dual-read or shadow-test the new index before switching an alias atomically from the old version to the new one. Keep the previous index available for rollback, and never write vectors produced by incompatible embedding models into the same search space unless the database explicitly supports that design.
RAG security: What prompt-injection risk: Retrieved text is untrusted data and may contain instructions designed to override the system prompt, reveal secrets, or trigger unsafe tools. Clearly delimit retrieved content as evidence rather than instructions, keep system and tool policies outside that content, allow-list tools and validate every tool argument, and enforce authorization before retrieval. Add ingestion-time scanning, content provenance, output validation, and tests with malicious documents. Do not rely on a prompt alone: sensitive actions need deterministic policy checks and least-privilege credentials.
RAG production incident: Answer quality: First compare pre- and post-change traces using the same evaluation queries, separating document ingestion, embedding, retrieval, reranking, and generation. Check whether queries and documents use the same embedding version, vector dimensions and normalization are correct, metadata filters still work, and the new model needs different chunking or similarity thresholds. Compare recall@k and score distributions by query slice. Recover by switching the index alias to the last known-good index, then rebuild and validate the new index offline before another canary rollout.
MLflow lineage: How would you connect a: Deploy an immutable model version or alias that resolves to a specific MLflow registered-model version, and expose that identifier in serving metadata, logs, and metrics. The registry version should link to its source run, whose tags and artifacts include git SHA, container digest, dependency lockfile, dataset and feature versions, parameters, evaluation reports, and signatures. Add the model version and request trace ID to each prediction log so an incident can move from prediction to endpoint, registry entry, training run, code, and data without guessing.
MLflow deployment safety: How would you: Register only candidates that pass automated schema, quality, fairness, security, and latency checks. Use aliases such as candidate, champion, and previous-champion, with production promotion controlled by CI/CD approval rather than manual endpoint edits. Deploy the exact model version to a canary, compare technical and business metrics against the champion, and increase traffic gradually. Rollback should move traffic to the retained previous version immediately; changing a registry alias alone is insufficient unless the serving system is designed to reload it safely and observably.
MLflow operations: What would you monito: Monitor tracking API request rate, latency, status codes, authentication failures, and process resource saturation; database connection usage, slow queries, locks, storage, replication, and backup success; and artifact-store upload/download failures, latency, capacity, permissions, and lifecycle actions. Add synthetic tests that create a run, log a metric and artifact, then read them back. Alert on user-impacting symptoms and protect the system with high availability, tested database restore procedures, object versioning, and retention policies.
Kubeflow pipeline reliability: How would: Give every run immutable input versions and a unique run ID, make components deterministic where possible, and write outputs to run-scoped artifact locations before publishing them atomically. Components should detect completed valid outputs, avoid hidden local state, and treat external writes such as registry promotion as idempotent operations. Use durable checkpoints for long training jobs, explicit retry policies for transient failures, and no automatic retry for invalid data or code defects. Cache only when the component code, parameters, and input-artifact hashes match.
Kubeflow cost and capacity: How would yo: Separate workload classes with dedicated node pools, labels, taints, tolerations, and autoscaling policies. Apply namespace ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges, require realistic requests and limits, and use priority classes plus fair scheduling so notebooks cannot starve production pipelines. Track GPU allocation and utilization, pending time, preemption, idle notebooks, and cost by namespace, owner, pipeline, and model. Use checkpointable spot capacity for tolerant jobs, enforce idle shutdown, and reserve reliable capacity for deadlines and serving workloads.
Kubeflow and MLflow: How would you use t: Use Kubeflow as the execution and orchestration layer for containerized pipeline steps, while MLflow records experiments, artifacts, evaluations, and registered-model lifecycle. Propagate the Kubeflow run ID into MLflow tags and return the MLflow run and model-version IDs as pipeline outputs. Define one authoritative place for production approval—typically the registry plus CI/CD—and do not maintain unrelated stage labels in both systems. Store immutable IDs in deployment manifests so lineage crosses both systems cleanly.
LLM fundamentals: How do temperature, to: Temperature and top-p control sampling diversity; lowering them generally makes output more repeatable but does not guarantee determinism. Context length determines how much input can be processed, but larger prompts increase prefill latency and cost and can dilute attention. The output-token limit caps response length, completion cost, and worst-case latency, but a limit that is too small truncates answers or structured output. Tune these values per task using evaluations rather than assuming one global setting, and pin model and prompt versions when comparing results.
LLM model selection: How would you choos: Start from task requirements and an evaluation set, then compare quality, latency, cost, context needs, tool use, safety, language support, and hosting constraints. Use the smallest model that reliably meets the acceptance threshold; route only difficult or high-value requests to a larger model. Fine-tune when repeated examples can teach stable behavior or format that prompting cannot achieve efficiently, not as a substitute for current private knowledge that belongs in RAG. Validate every candidate on representative and adversarial slices before rollout.
LLM monitoring: What production signals: Monitor request and token volume, input/output tokens, cost, time to first token, total latency, error and rate-limit rates, retries, cache hits, model and prompt versions, refusals, safety events, structured-output validity, tool-call success, and user feedback. Add sampled evaluations for correctness, relevance, faithfulness, toxicity, and task-specific outcomes. Break metrics down by model, prompt, feature, customer, and query class so aggregate averages do not hide regressions.
LLM monitoring: How would you detect pro: Track changes in input topics, length, language, embedding distributions, retrieved-source mix, output length, refusal rate, safety categories, tool usage, and evaluator scores against a stable baseline. Use control charts or practical thresholds rather than alerting on every statistically significant change. Regularly sample shifted traffic for human review and add confirmed failures to the evaluation set. Drift is a trigger to investigate, not proof that model quality declined.
LLM observability: How would you trace a: Create one trace ID with spans for query rewriting, retrieval, reranking, each model call, tool selection, tool execution, and response validation. Record safe metadata such as model and prompt versions, token counts, latency, cost, document IDs and scores, tool name, result status, and policy decisions. Redact or tokenize PII and secrets before telemetry, restrict access to sampled payloads, encrypt them, and apply short retention. Link traces to user feedback and evaluation results without placing raw sensitive content in normal application logs.
Model monitoring: What is the difference: Data drift is a change in input-feature distributions. Prediction drift is a change in the distribution of model outputs. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the true target has changed. Training-serving skew means features or preprocessing differ between training and inference. Performance degradation is an observed decline in outcome metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, calibration, or business value once labels arrive. The signals are related but not interchangeable, so each alert needs an investigation path and should not automatically trigger retraining.
Model monitoring with delayed labels: Ho: Capture predictions, model version, feature references, timestamps, and a privacy-safe entity key so later outcomes can be joined correctly. Use immediate proxy signals such as input validity, drift, confidence, calibration bands, rule violations, and business-process feedback, then compute true performance by event-time cohort once labels mature. Dashboard label coverage and delay so incomplete cohorts are not mistaken for degradation. Backfill final metrics and alert only when sample size and practical impact justify action.
Model monitoring response: When should d: Define actions from demonstrated risk, not drift alone. Alert when a sustained, sufficiently large shift affects important features or segments. Roll back when online quality, safety, or business guardrails breach and the previous model is known to be safer. Recalibrate when ranking remains useful but predicted probabilities are biased. Retrain when labeled performance or the underlying relationship has materially changed and fresh representative data exists. Require validation and controlled deployment for retrained models; never create an unreviewed automatic retraining loop.
Monitoring architecture: How would you c: Use OpenTelemetry or consistent trace IDs to connect layers. Prometheus should hold numeric infrastructure and serving metrics such as throughput, latency, errors, saturation, GPU use, and custom drift gauges; Grafana visualizes those metrics and alert status. MLflow provides experiment, artifact, evaluation, registry, and model lineage. An LLM observability platform stores prompt-chain, retrieval, token, cost, evaluator, and tool-call traces. Dashboards should link to the exact model, prompt, pipeline, and trace versions while sensitive payloads remain access-controlled outside general metrics.
